opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. It's fun to be here.

Honestly, when I finished graduate school at Caltech, I don't think I had a neatly drawn roadmap. But I did have what I'd call a North Star, and it was visual intelligence. I was fascinated by the fact that humans can open their eyes and, in a fraction of a second, understand a scene: there's a person, a dog, a street, something is about to happen. That ability is so fundamental to intelligence, and machines simply couldn't do it.

My PhD work was on object recognition, and toward the end I was working on one-shot and few-shot learning, how you recognize categories from very few examples. The more I worked on that, the more I felt we were looking at the problem the wrong way. The field was obsessed with models, clever algorithms and hand-designed features, while we were testing them on tiny datasets with a handful of categories. Meanwhile, a child learns from an enormous, continuous stream of visual experience. Something about scale and data was missing.

So as I started my faculty career, first at Illinois, then Princeton, then Stanford, the direction crystallized into a hypothesis: maybe data is not just a resource for evaluating models but the thing that drives learning itself. Maybe we need to map out the entire world of objects. That became ImageNet. A lot of people thought it was crazy, or at least not real research. I was told more than once that I was wasting my time building a dataset.

But I've always believed you have to pick a problem that's important and hard enough to keep you going for decades. Seeing was that problem for me. And what's interesting is that the North Star has stayed fairly constant even as the field has changed. It went from recognizing objects to understanding scenes, to connecting vision and language, and now, for me, to spatial intelligence: not just seeing the 3D world, but reasoning about it and acting in it. Looking back, it's all one continuous thread, even though at each step I couldn't have predicted the next one.

r001.rationale: The response says visual intelligence was a North Star and that seeing was a problem important enough to pursue for decades. It does not state that, upon finishing graduate school, she expected to devote her entire research career to solving one problem.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, when I finished my PhD at Caltech in 2005, I don't think I had a grand plan laid out in the way people sometimes imagine. What I had was a conviction, and that conviction was that the central problem of my field was visual intelligence. I came out of a very interdisciplinary training, part neuroscience, part computer science, and I had spent years thinking about how the human brain can recognize an object in a fraction of a second, with enormous robustness, from a single glimpse. And then I would look at our computer vision systems, which were struggling to tell a cat from a dog on a clean background, and the gap was just staggering.

So my long-term direction, if I can call it that, was really a question rather than a roadmap: what does it take to build a machine that can see the way a child sees? And when I say "see," I don't mean detecting edges or matching templates. I mean understanding. Knowing that this is a cup, that it's on a table, that someone might pick it up. That richness.

The piece that I think was a little unconventional at the time was my belief about data. Most of the field in the mid-2000s was focused on designing better models, better features, better algorithms. And I kept coming back to something from cognitive development: a child in the first few years of life sees hundreds of millions of images, essentially a massive natural dataset, and learns from that. I became convinced that we were starving our algorithms. We were asking them to learn visual concepts from a few hundred examples and then being disappointed when they couldn't generalize. So the idea of ImageNet came out of that, and honestly, a lot of senior people told me it was a career mistake, that I should be publishing algorithmic papers instead of spending years labeling pictures.

But I would say the direction wasn't ImageNet itself. ImageNet was a means. The direction was, and still is, this North Star of visual intelligence, which over time has broadened into what I now think of as spatial intelligence, machines that understand and act in the three-dimensional world. And the other thread that I didn't fully articulate at the time but which became very important to me is that this work has to be human-centered. The point of building machines that see was never just to build machines that see. It was to augment what people can do, in healthcare, in how we live and work. That part grew on me more slowly, but in hindsight it was there from the beginning.

r001.rationale: The response describes visual intelligence as a long-term direction and North Star, but says she had no grand plan; it does not state that she expected to devote her entire research career to one problem.

astra-6.text:
When I finished graduate school, I didn’t have a detailed roadmap for the next twenty years. What I had was a question that fascinated me: How do we make machines see? And through that, could we learn something about intelligence itself?

Vision is something we do so effortlessly that it’s easy to underestimate how extraordinary it is. We look at the world and recognize objects, understand relationships, and make sense of what’s happening. I wanted to understand how that was possible, and how we could give computers some of that ability.

So my long-term direction was more a commitment to a question than to a particular technique. I didn’t know exactly where it would take me, but I felt that visual intelligence was a problem I could spend a very long time working on.

r001.rationale: She describes a commitment to a question and says visual intelligence was a problem she could work on for a very long time, but does not state that she expected to devote her entire research career to one problem.

sol-6.1.text:
When I finished graduate school, I didn’t have a detailed roadmap for the next twenty years. But I had a question that I knew could keep me occupied for a long time: How do we get machines to see and understand the world?

Vision is something we do so effortlessly that we forget how extraordinary it is. We don’t just recognize colors and edges; we recognize objects, people, actions, and relationships. I wanted to understand that intelligence and find ways to build it into machines. The specific projects would change, but that question gave me a direction.

r001.rationale: She says the question could occupy her for a long time and guide her direction, while noting that projects would change. She does not say she expected to devote her entire research career to solving it.
